title: How to count threads for evenweave cross-stitch
subtitle: Working over two threads on linen or evenweave instead of Aida squares
excerpt: Evenweave fabric has no built-in squares like Aida; each stitch is worked over a counted number of individual fabric threads. Cross-stitch on evenweave is typically worked over two threads in each direction, giving a stitch size equivalent to 28-count evenweave stitched over two threads equal to 14-count Aida. Counting threads accurately determines whether the stitches are correctly spaced.
sourceNotes: Thread counting for evenweave cross-stitch on linen. Weldon's Practical Needlework series (1880s), Internet Archive. Standard guidance in major cross-stitch publisher guides.

glossaryTerms.definition: The six-strand embroidery thread used for cross-stitch.
A stiff, evenly-woven cross-stitch fabric with clearly visible squares formed by groups of threads.

content.text: Evenweave fabric does not have the pre-formed squares of

. Instead, the stitcher counts individual warp and weft threads, entering the needle between specific threads to form each stitch. The most common approach is to work each cross-stitch over two threads in each direction, which creates a stitch the same size as a single Aida square at half the thread count.
Counting and stitching over two threads

Hold the evenweave fabric up to the light. The individual warp threads (running lengthwise) and weft threads (running crosswise) should be clearly visible and evenly spaced. Count two warp threads from your starting position and two weft threads to establish the boundaries of the first stitch.
Bring the needle up between the 2nd and 3rd warp threads, and between the 2nd and 3rd weft threads from the lower-left of the first stitch. This position is the lower-left hole of your first stitch.
Insert the needle into the fabric two warp threads to the right and two weft threads up from where you emerged. This diagonal span over two threads in each direction is the first leg of the cross.
Complete the cross by returning from lower-right to upper-left over the same two-by-two thread span. The
should lie smooth over exactly two threads in each direction, and the cross should be square.

Check the stitch count after the first row. Hold the piece at arm's length and verify the stitches are evenly spaced and the row runs straight along the weave. Stitches that drift higher or lower than two threads indicate a counting error; unpick and recount before continuing.

items.symptom: Stitches are not square — they look wider or taller than expected
items.cause: The thread count was not consistent: some stitches span three threads in one direction and two in the other.
items.fix: Count carefully before each stitch. On fine evenweave, a needle threader or tapestry needle makes it easier to push between specific threads without splitting them. Work under good light and use a magnifying glass on very fine counts.

items.symptom: The needle splits the evenweave threads rather than passing between them
items.cause: A sharp needle is catching the fine threads rather than pushing between them.
items.fix: Use a blunt tapestry needle. The rounded tip pushes between the threads rather than piercing them. On very fine evenweave (32-count and above) a size 28 tapestry needle is appropriate.

content.text: Evenweave gives a finer result than Aida for the same chart because the individual thread count is higher. A design stitched on 28-count evenweave over two threads produces the same stitch size as 14-count Aida, but the background fabric is softer and more translucent. Evenweave is also suitable for projects that will be washed repeatedly, as it does not have the starch sizing of Aida.
